2g16e32jqy4: ## Two levers, two levels of control
el7qcwp35q: Intune manages security through two levers. **MDM** (mobile device management): the device is **enrolled**, Intune installs an MDM certificate on it and can enforce configuration, compliance and enrollment policies across the whole device. **MAM** (mobile application management): the device is not enrolled, and Intune protects the **data inside specific applications** (Outlook, Teams) through app protection policies. MDM controls the container, MAM controls the content. The two can be combined on a corporate device that needs additional protection on certain applications.
2bq5aphlfou: ## Device ownership and the choice of enrollment
225jh95j5uc: The question that decides everything is **ownership**. A corporate device is managed in depth: on Apple, **Automated Device Enrollment (ADE)** yields a **supervised** device (updates through MDM, restrictions, application blocking); on Android, the fully managed, corporate-owned work profile or dedicated modes; on Windows, Autopilot or enrollment by Entra join. A personal device (BYOD) is managed with restraint: on iOS and iPadOS, **account-driven enrollment** (iOS 13 and later) configures a limited set of work features and applications, or device enrollment with Company Portal; on Android, the work profile; on macOS, user-approved enrollment. For users who refuse to enroll their device, **MAM without enrollment** (Android, iOS/iPadOS, Windows) protects access to email and Teams. Classic trap: applying the expectations of a supervised device to a BYOD. Data protection is limited by what the enrollment mode actually allows.

Other points: a device managed by **another MDM provider** must first be removed, and a corporate device on Apple (ADE), Android fully managed, corporate-owned or dedicated requires a **factory reset** to switch MDM, whereas BYOD does not. On macOS, there is no Company Portal in the App Store: the user downloads the installation package.

qlz5geiq3t: An Intune role is a set of permissions (management categories such as "Device configurations" and actions such as read, create, update, delete, assign). A role is **assigned to groups**, not to people. An assignment specifies the **members** (the administrators), the **scope (groups)** (the users and devices on which the rights apply) and the **scope tags**. Permissions from several groups are **cumulative** and there is **no deny option**. Consequence: an excess of assignments can only be corrected by removal.

131ji8gleik: ## Several paths to the same settings
4tjkmmh1qa: In Intune, the same security setting can often be set through **several paths**: an **Endpoint security** policy (antivirus, firewall, encryption, attack surface reduction, EDR, account protection), a **settings catalog** profile (the list of all available settings, for example all BitLocker settings), a **template** (logical groups such as VPN, Wi-Fi, kiosk), a **security baseline** (a preconfigured set of Windows settings, recommended by security teams) or a **compliance policy** that evaluates the state. No path is "the right one" in itself: what matters is to decide on **one path per setting** before deploying.
1jca7vso237: Endpoint security policies are organized by function. They are task-centered ("I configure the antivirus") and managing them requires the **Endpoint Security Manager** role or equivalent rights. They fit when a security team separate from the endpoint management team owns these settings, because RBAC can separate them. Microsoft best practice: use Endpoint security policies **or** baselines for the same settings, not both.
5i8t0b6wtc: The catalog is the modern approach for Windows and macOS: you search for a setting by name and configure it. It distinguishes **device-scope** from **user-scope** settings, which influences the assignment. It is the right choice for a setting missing from the Endpoint security policies, or when you want all the settings of a feature together. The catalog also imports GPOs through group policy analytics, with detection of conflicts between GPOs at the migration stage.
vz3mhm1ngt: A baseline applies dozens of settings with recommended values (for example, enable BitLocker for removable drives, require an unlock password, disable basic authentication). You **customize** it to keep only the values you want. Points to know: new versions do **not automatically overwrite** existing profiles, whose settings become **read-only**; updating to the latest version creates a **new instance** in parallel, with the choice to **keep** or **discard** the customizations; **scope tags and assignments are not carried over** and must be redone on the new instance. The format changed in May 2023: profiles created before follow their own migration process. Before an update, **download the differences report** (CSV) to see the settings added, removed or whose default value changes, and test on a pilot group.
22q6wtftckk: A simple table avoids surprises: for each key setting, which policy type owns it, which group receives it, which owner maintains it. Without this, a new administrator adds an "equivalent" policy that conflicts with the first.

Basic principle: the **included** or **excluded** Entra groups are a starting point; the group is the limiting factor, so use the smallest possible scope, then **refine with an assignment filter**. A filter is a reusable rule, based on a property of the device or application (operating system, version, manufacturer, model, ownership, category), evaluated at enrollment and at each device check-in, in **include** or **exclude** mode. Limits to remember: 200 filters per tenant, 3,072 characters per filter, enrolled devices for managed devices; for managed applications, filters apply to app protection and app configuration policies, but not to compliance policies or device configuration profiles (check the list of supported workloads for your case).

1npwx43h96h: It would be wrong to say that one policy type always wins. According to the documentation, the rule depends on the **types involved**, setting by setting. (1) **Compliance versus configuration**: when the same setting appears in a compliance policy and in a configuration policy (Endpoint security, baseline, device configuration), the value of the **compliance policy** is the one retained. (2) **Several compliance policies**: the **most restrictive** value applies. (3) **Several configuration policies** (Endpoint security, baselines, device configuration, catalog): different values for the same setting create a **conflict to resolve manually**; the setting may not apply and is reported as in conflict. (4) **App protection policies**: conflicting values resolve to the most restrictive value, except for numeric fields, and the first policy deployed keeps precedence. (5) **Custom Apple profiles**: Intune does not evaluate the content of an Apple configuration file or of a custom OMA-URI, which is only a vehicle; in case of conflict between them, Apple applies the settings randomly. Conclusion: read the reports setting by setting, do not guess.
